description: Equipo que busca aprender cosas nuevas, divertirse conociendo a otros y sobre todo no cometer nuestros errores del pasado
summary: Lunar Survival Simulator is an educational web game for children aged 7 to 12. Players run a moon base for 5 days: they share out electricity with switches and decide which systems to keep on, because every watt, liter of water and gram of oxygen is limited, as in NASA's Artemis missions. Random events (solar storms, leaks, micrometeoroids) damage food, water, oxygen or radiation protection, and players fix them with four science mini-games: LED-light photosynthesis, water recycling with pipes, water electrolysis to make oxygen, and a space-weather radar that uses real NASA DONKI data. Kids learn that in space every decision has a cost. It runs in any browser, with nothing to install, in Spanish and English.
details:
What it does and how it works. Players operate a moon base for 5 days (06:00 to 20:00) and watch five critical fields: food, water, oxygen, radiation and electricity. Electricity is the central resource: every switch that is on uses it, and it recharges each day, so players must decide which system to keep running. Each day has its own identity (from an adaptation day to a massive solar storm). Events warn players before they happen, sometimes offer a choice between a quick patch and a full repair, and damage a sector that keeps degrading until the player wins its mini-game: calibrating the red and blue light of a greenhouse (food), connecting pipes to the filter (water), tuning the voltage of an electrolysis cell (oxygen), or raising the shields just as a radiation wave arrives (space-weather radar). If faults remain at the end of the day, there is a 20-second extension before the mission is lost.

Benefits and expected impact. It teaches, through play, that resources in space are limited and that every decision involves a trade-off, together with real concepts: photosynthesis, water recycling, electrolysis and space weather. It uses real NASA data (DONKI): the strongest solar flare of the last 30 days sets the risk of the radiation mini-game. It is free and runs in the browser, with no accounts or installation.

Tools and technology. Plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript with ES modules (no frameworks), the Web Audio API for synthesized sounds, the NASA DONKI API with a local backup if the network fails, Git and GitHub for a team of 5, and Vercel for hosting. Icons (Fluent Emoji) and fonts (Fredoka, Orbitron and Chakra Petch) are open source and bundled with the project. The data structures are implemented from scratch: a linked list for the mission days, an adjacency graph with BFS and DFS for the pipe mini-game (every generated level is solvable) and a priority queue for the event scheduler. They are verified with 55 automated tests.

Creativity. It combines resource management with real science and real NASA data in a format designed for children: advance warnings, risky decisions, adaptive difficulty in every mini-game, upgrades chosen between days, achievements and scoring.

Factors the team considered. An audience of 7 to 12 year olds (slow clock, gentle consumption and short texts); Spanish and English versions; privacy (no accounts or sign-up, and the browser stores preferences only if functional cookies are accepted); working even without a connection to the NASA API thanks to backup data; and open licenses for every external resource.

Use of artificial intelligence. Part of the game core code (clock, energy and mission days, module integration, data structures and automated tests) and the documentation were developed with help from the AI assistant Claude (Anthropic); this is stated in the README and in file headers. The game contains no AI-generated images, audio or video: icons are Microsoft Fluent Emoji and sounds are synthesized in code. [COMPLETE: if other team members used AI in their modules, say so here.]
